passage:
You know Bhavna from my team? Everyone calls her arrogant. In every meeting she finds a way to mention the award, the client who asked for her by name, the report the director loved. People roll their eyes.
I used to as well. Then one day I saw her before a review, rereading her own old appreciation emails in the pantry, lips moving. That didn't look like arrogance. It looked like someone checking she was still good enough.
So I started saying specific things. "Your summary on slide four made the numbers clear." Just that, once a week or so. And it's odd, but this last month she has brought up the award maybe once. Last Thursday she even asked, "Himani, how did you build that spreadsheet?"

qa.q: What did Himani see Bhavna doing in the pantry?
qa.a: Bhavna was rereading her own old appreciation emails, lips moving.

qa.q: What did Himani think Bhavna's listing of achievements was really about?
qa.a: Himani read it as a need for reassurance, like someone checking she was still good enough, more than arrogance.

qa.q: What small step did Himani take, and how did it help?
qa.a: Himani gave specific, honest praise about once a week, and Bhavna mentioned the award far less and even asked Himani for help.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel when she hears "Your summary on slide four made the numbers clear"?
qa.a: She likely feels truly seen for real work, which eases her need to prove herself by listing wins.

grounding: A coworker sees a peer's constant listing of achievements as hunger for reassurance and finds that specific acknowledgement lowers the bragging.

passage:
Our theatre group rehearses every Sunday in the community hall, and Abhinav has a habit. Whenever the director gives him a note, within five minutes he mentions the three college plays he led, or the newspaper line that once called him "promising". The others exchange looks.
Last week I watched more closely. The listing always came right after a correction, never after praise. His voice went fast and bright, and his eyes kept checking our faces. I can't be sure, but it looked less like pride and more like someone patching a hole.
So after the run-through I told him, "That pause before your last line gave me goosebumps." He blinked. "Really? Thanks, Parveen." For the rest of the evening, he didn't mention college once.

qa.q: When did Abhinav usually mention his college plays?
qa.a: Within five minutes of the director giving him a note, right after a correction.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel about Abhinav's listing, and why?
qa.a: Parveen felt curious and sympathetic, sensing insecurity like someone patching a hole, because the listing always followed a correction and his eyes kept checking faces.

qa.q: What did Parveen try, and what happened?
qa.a: Parveen gave a specific compliment about his pause before the last line, and Abhinav didn't mention college for the rest of the evening.

qa.q: What might it be like for Abhinav to receive the director's notes?
qa.a: Corrections may sting and make him worry he isn't good enough, so he reaches for old successes to feel steady.

grounding: A member of a theatre group notices a peer's boasting follows every correction, reads it as insecurity, and eases it with specific praise.

passage:
Monday. Harish joined Imran's analytics team from another city. At lunch, before anyone asked, he listed his old company's awards, two certifications and the dashboard his old boss had "shown to the whole board." Imran noticed that while he talked, Harish kept turning his spoon over and over.
Thursday. In the team meeting, Harish again explained his past projects, this time to people who had not asked. A senior colleague rolled her eyes. Imran didn't. He was thinking of his own first month, and how scared he had been of looking like the new guy who knew nothing.
The next Tuesday, Harish's query fixed a bug that had slowed their reports for weeks. Imran stopped by his desk. "The way you rewrote that join was really clean. It saved me an hour today."
Harish looked up, surprised, and simply said, "Thanks." That afternoon, for the first time, he asked a question instead of listing an award.

qa.q: What did Harish keep doing with his spoon at lunch?
qa.a: He kept turning his spoon over and over.

qa.q: Why didn't Imran roll his eyes in the meeting?
qa.a: Imran felt sympathy, remembering how scared he had been in his own first month, so he read Harish's listing as insecurity rather than arrogance.

qa.q: Which choice helped Harish, and why?
qa.a: Imran's specific praise for the rewritten join worked, because real acknowledgement eased Harish's need to prove himself.

qa.q: How might Harish have felt when Imran praised the query?
qa.a: Harish probably felt surprised and relieved, finally seen for current work, which let him ask a question instead of listing awards.

grounding: It shows a colleague reading a peer's repeated listing of achievements as a hunger for reassurance and using specific acknowledgement to ease it.

passage:
Nirmala, you're complaining about the new manager who talks only about his old wins. Let me, Darshan, tell you about the first year I worked at the bank.
A colleague joined our branch. Every tea break, he told us about his gold medal from college, his quick promotion, his letter of praise. The others started avoiding the tea room.
I watched him more carefully. When he talked about medals, his voice went faster, and he never finished his tea. It didn't look like pride to me. It looked like fear, as if he was proving he belonged.
One day, he quietly caught a mistake in a loan file that would have cost a family dearly. I told him, in front of the manager, "You saw what three of us missed. Thank you."
He went red. After that, he talked less about the medal and more about the files. Sometimes that's all people need, Nirmala. To be seen for today.

qa.q: What mistake did the colleague catch?
qa.a: He caught a mistake in a loan file that would have cost a family dearly.

qa.q: What did young Darshan feel as he watched the colleague closely?
qa.a: Darshan felt curious and sympathetic, sensing fear rather than pride behind the fast talk about medals.

qa.q: At what turning point did the colleague's bragging ease?
qa.a: When Darshan thanked him specifically, in front of the manager, for catching the loan file mistake.

qa.q: How might the colleague have felt when Darshan thanked him?
qa.a: He likely felt embarrassed but deeply reassured, seen for his present work, which reduced his need to talk about medals.

grounding: A senior colleague recalls reading a peer's constant listing of achievements as insecurity and easing it with specific acknowledgement.

passage:
The client was arriving in ten minutes, the conference room projector had just died, and Ira would not stop talking.
"You know I did the Singapore rollout, right? And the award last year? And the client in Mumbai asked for me specially."
Aparna, fighting with the projector cable, looked at her. Ira's hands were shaking as she shuffled her printouts. This was her first big pitch at the new firm. The others on the team had already started calling her "Miss Award."
Aparna put the cable down. "Ira. Your slide on their delivery delays is the best thing in this deck. It's the first thing I'd show them."
Ira stopped mid-sentence. "Really?"
"Really. You understood their problem better than we did."
Ira took a breath and nodded. When the client walked in, she led with the delay slide on a printed sheet and didn't mention a single award.

qa.q: What had just died in the conference room?
qa.a: The conference room projector had just died.

qa.q: What did Aparna feel when she noticed Ira's shaking hands?
qa.a: Aparna noticed Ira's shaking hands and felt concern, reading the listing of awards as nervousness about her first big pitch, not arrogance.

qa.q: What worked better than ignoring or teasing Ira?
qa.a: Aparna's specific praise of the delivery-delay slide calmed Ira, so she focused on the client instead of past awards.

qa.q: How does Ira feel after Aparna's words?
qa.a: Ira feels steadier and reassured, able to lead with her real work and stop listing awards.

grounding: It shows a colleague under pressure reading a peer's bragging as a hunger for reassurance and lowering it with specific acknowledgement.

passage:
In the Pune office, Ankita had a way of turning every conversation back to her record. The award in 2022. The client who asked for her by name. The certification she'd finished in six weeks. At lunch the others traded glances.
Jeevan noticed something else. She did it most right after the manager talked over her in meetings, and her voice always sped up, as if she was afraid of being interrupted.
On Friday, after her presentation, he stopped by her desk. "The way you broke down the vendor costs on slide four was really clear. I'm going to steal that format."
Ankita looked startled. "Oh. Thanks." She didn't list anything else.
Over the next few weeks, Jeevan made a point of naming specific things she did well. He noticed she mentioned 2022 less and less. One day she even asked him about his project first.

qa.q: What did Jeevan praise about Ankita's presentation?
qa.a: The way she broke down the vendor costs on slide four.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel about Ankita's listing of achievements, and why?
qa.a: Jeevan felt concern rather than irritation, reading the boasting as a hunger for reassurance, since it came right after being talked over in meetings.

qa.q: What approach did Jeevan use, and what changed?
qa.a: He gave kind, specific acknowledgement of real work, and over the following weeks Ankita mentioned past awards less and asked about others more.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt when Jeevan praised slide four?
qa.a: Ankita was startled and quietly pleased, perhaps feeling truly seen for once, so she didn't need to list anything else.

grounding: Shows a colleague reading a peer's constant boasting as a need for reassurance and easing it with kind, specific acknowledgement.
